steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm married filing jointly in Phoenix AZ. W-2 from Riverside Hospital: $79,400. Additional income: $12,500 (consulting, 6 clients), $920 from Goldman Sachs Marcus, $480 from TD Ameritrade. Home office: 140 sq ft exclusive; I pay $2,100/month for 690 sq ft. Deductions: $3,600 student loan interest (MOHELA, 2016–2019); $1,400 to Northwest Harvest (food bank) have the receipt; $950 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
I can help — here’s a clear, practical summary of what looks deductible from the information you gave, how to treat the home office, whether you’ll likely itemize, and the forms you’ll need. Quick disclaimer: I’m not a CPA — this is general guidance. If your situation is complex I recommend confirming with a tax pro.

What’s deductible (federal) from the items you gave
- W‑2 wages (Riverside Hospital $79,400): report on Form 1040 (wages shown on W‑2).
- Consulting $12,500: report as self‑employment income on Schedule C if you were an independent contractor (1099‑NEC or similar). If you were an employee and it was unreimbursed, different rules apply — see questions below.
- Interest income: $920 (Goldman Sachs Marcus) + $480 (TD Ameritrade) = $1,400. Taxable as interest on Form 1040 (Schedule B only required if total taxable interest/dividends > $1,500).
- Student loan interest: only interest actually paid during the tax year may be deductible (up to $2,500 maximum, subject to income phaseouts). You reported $3,600 — only up to $2,500 can be claimed as the above‑the‑line student loan interest deduction, and that amount may be reduced/eliminated if your modified AGI is above the phaseout threshold. Based on the income you gave (~$93k) you are likely below the MFJ phaseout start, so you should be able to claim up to $2,500 — but confirm the $3,600 is interest paid in the tax year being filed.
- Charitable cash donation $1,400: deductible if you itemize (must be to a qualified charity and you have the receipt).
- Unreimbursed expenses $950: 
  - If these are employee unreimbursed expenses (for a W‑2 job), they are generally NOT deductible for tax years after 2017 (suspended miscellaneous itemized deductions).
  - If the $950 are business expenses related to the consulting/self‑employed work, deduct them on Schedule C.

Home office treatment
- You said: office 140 sq ft exclusive, home 690 sq ft → business-use percentage = 140/690 ≈ 20.29%.
- Two methods:
  1. Simplified method: $5 per sq ft up to 300 sq ft → 140 × $5 = $700 deduction on Schedule C.
  2. Actual expenses method: allocate a percentage of actual home expenses to the business. Example using your rent:
     - Rent = $2,100/mo × 12 = $25,200/year.
     - Home office portion of rent = 25,200 × 20.29% ≈ $5,114.
     - You can also allocate utilities, renter’s insurance, other direct/indirect eligible costs. The actual method often gives a larger deduction when rent or mortgage interest is significant.
- If you take the actual method, compute Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) and attach results to Schedule C. If you use the simplified method, you do not file Form 8829.
- Important: Home office deduction is available only if the space is used regularly and exclusively for business and if the consulting is self‑employment (Schedule C). Employees cannot claim this deduction on Schedule A for tax years after 2017.

Self‑employment tax and related adjustments
- If the $12,500 is self‑employment income (Schedule C), you’ll pay self‑employment tax (Social Security + Medicare) on net earnings — roughly 15.3% of net self‑employment earnings (the calculation uses 92.35% of net profit). You may also deduct half of your self‑employment tax as an adjustment to income on Schedule 1.
- Example ballpark with actual home office (rent portion) and the $950 business cost:
  - Gross consulting 12,500 − home office rent share ≈ 5,114 − $950 = net profit ≈ $6,436
  - SE taxable earnings ≈ 0.9235 × 6,436 ≈ 5,945 → SE tax ≈ 5,945 × 15.3% ≈ $909
  - Half SE tax deductible (adjustment) ≈ $454
  (This is illustrative — exact numbers depend on other business expenses you may have.)

Itemize vs standard deduction
- For 2024 (filed in 2025) the standard deduction for Married Filing Jointly will be higher than in prior years — (confirm the exact IRS inflation‑adjusted amount when filing). To decide:
  - Itemized deductions would include charitable gifts ($1,400), state & local taxes paid (SALT) up to $10,000, mortgage interest (if any), property taxes, and other allowable items.
  - From the items you listed, the only clear itemized amount is $1,400 charity. Unless you have substantial state/local taxes, mortgage interest, or other itemizable expenses exceeding the standard deduction, you’ll likely take the standard deduction.
- Bottom line: With only $1,400 in charity and no mortgage interest listed, you’re probably better off taking the standard deduction — unless SALT + other itemizable expenses push your total above the standard amount.

Forms you will likely need
- Form 1040 (U.S. Individual Income Tax Return).
- Schedule 1 (additional income/adjustments) — for student loan interest adjustment (and other adjustments).
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss From Business) — to report consulting income and business expenses (including the home office).
- Schedule SE (Self‑Employment Tax) — to compute SE tax.
- Form 8829 — if you use the actual expense method for the home office (attach to Schedule C). Not needed if you use the simplified method.
- Schedule A — only if you decide to itemize deductions.
- 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC (for consulting income) — include amounts even if you did not receive a 1099 but you received income.
- 1099‑INT (interest income) and 1098‑E (student loan interest statement) — use these to report interest and to substantiate student loan interest paid.
- Keep receipts and records (charity receipt, rent payments, utility bills, records for business expenses, records proving exclusive use of office).

Questions I need to confirm or that will change the answer
1. Was the $12,500 consulting income paid to you as an independent contractor (1099‑NEC) or as a W‑2 employee? (If W‑2 employee, the home office/business deductions are treated very differently.)
2. Is the $3,600 student loan interest amount the interest you actually paid during the tax year you’re filing for (2024), or is that an aggregated total for earlier years? (Only interest paid in the tax year is deductible.)
3. Are the $950 “unreimbursed expenses” employee expenses, or were they business expenses related to the consulting work?
4. Do you have any mortgage interest, property taxes, or substantial state and local taxes paid in 2024? This affects whether itemizing beats the standard deduction.
5. Do you want me to run an estimated tax/return calculation using the numbers above (I can show estimated taxable income, federal income tax, SE tax, and compare itemize vs. standard with any additional figures you provide)?

Next steps I can do for you
- If you confirm the answers to the questions above (especially whether consulting is self‑employment and whether the $3,600 was paid in the filing year), I can:
  - Run a quick estimate showing (a) standard deduction vs. itemized with the figures you have, and (b) expected self‑employment tax and net tax.
  - Draft a checklist of documents to gather before filing or sending to a tax pro.
  - Draft an email to your CPA with the facts and numbers, if you want me to.

Tell me which of the clarifying questions above applies and whether you want the quick estimate/calculation — I’ll run the numbers for you.
